text: Some assertions are specific to your business, not reusable across projects — refunds are negative, so an order's total should never go negative. That's not something dbt could ship as a built-in. A singular test fills that gap: a one-off SQL query you write yourself.

A singular test is just a .sql file in the tests/ directory. Same rule as generic tests: it's a select statement, and if it returns any rows, those rows are the failures. The test's name comes straight from its filename.
This is dbt Labs' own published example. Group payments by order, sum the amount, return any order where that sum went negative. One row back means a real order_id to debug with, in hand.

Since a singular test isn't declared in a model's schema.yml, it gets its own small YAML entry in tests/schema.yml if you want a description — data_tests, name, description, same as any other dbt resource.
Next lesson: schema.yml & Column-Level Documentation — where tests and descriptions live side by side.
